PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 77 — Lesson 101: Peripheral Artery Disease Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize peripheral artery disease (PAD) across its clinical spectrum, distinguish stable claudication from limb-threatening ischemia, use appropriate diagnostic reasoning, reduce cardiovascular and limb risk, and coordinate foot care and vascular referral safely.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate asymptomatic PAD, chronic symptomatic PAD, chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and acute limb ischemia (ALI).
  • Use history and focused vascular/foot examination to distinguish vascular claudication from neurogenic, musculoskeletal, venous, and neuropathic symptoms.
  • Explain the role and limitations of the ankle-brachial index (ABI) in suspected PAD.
  • Integrate tobacco treatment, lipid/BP/diabetes management, antithrombotic safety, structured exercise, and foot care into risk reduction.
  • Recognize urgent limb-threat and emergency ALI findings requiring immediate escalation.

Part 1 — PAD Is Both a Limb Disease and a Cardiovascular-Risk Marker

PAD reflects atherosclerotic disease outside the coronary circulation and commonly affects the lower extremities. It may be asymptomatic, cause chronic exertional leg symptoms, progress to CLTI, or present abruptly as ALI. Even people without classic claudication can have increased risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, tissue loss, and amputation. Therefore, a “leg circulation” visit must also address global atherosclerotic risk.

Part 2 — History: Do Not Reduce Every Leg Symptom to Claudication

Classic claudication is reproducible muscle discomfort with walking or exertion that resolves with rest. Ask where it occurs, the walking distance that triggers it, whether the threshold changes, what relieves it, and how it limits work, shopping, stairs, and independence. Also ask about rest pain, nocturnal pain relieved by dependency, nonhealing wounds, color/temperature change, prior revascularization, tobacco, diabetes, CKD, neuropathy, heart failure, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, and foot-care access.

Consider neurogenic claudication (often posture-related and relieved by flexion), osteoarthritis or musculoskeletal pain, venous disease, neuropathy, radiculopathy, medication-associated myopathy, and deconditioning. PAD and another cause can coexist. A normal-looking skin color or a patient’s ability to walk slowly does not exclude PAD.

Part 3 — Focused Examination and ABI

Examine both legs and feet: pulses, capillary refill in context, temperature, color, dependent rubor, elevation pallor, hair/skin changes, edema, wounds, infection, sensation, footwear, callus, and signs of neuropathy. Compare sides and document change from baseline. A resting ABI is a recommended test to establish PAD in patients with history or examination findings suggestive of disease. ABI results must be interpreted with the entire presentation; calcified/noncompressible vessels can make interpretation more complex, especially in diabetes or CKD, and additional physiologic testing may be needed.

Part 4 — Recognize the Two Limb-Threat Patterns

Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) is chronic severe PAD with ischemic rest pain, nonhealing wound/ulcer, or gangrene. It threatens tissue and requires prompt vascular and multidisciplinary evaluation; infection and diabetes can accelerate harm. Do not manage a painful, nonhealing ischemic-appearing foot ulcer as “routine podiatry follow-up” without assessing perfusion and urgency.

Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a sudden decrease in arterial perfusion threatening limb viability. Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis/weakness, and poikilothermia/coolness are classic warning features, but do not wait for all of them. Sudden limb symptoms, especially neurologic deficits or a cold/pulseless extremity, require emergency evaluation and immediate vascular coordination.

Part 5 — Longitudinal Risk Reduction

PAD management includes guideline-directed lipid lowering, blood-pressure control, diabetes management, tobacco cessation, antiplatelet/antithrombotic decisions tailored to the indication and bleeding risk, physical activity, and preventive foot care. Medication choices must account for kidney function, bleeding history, atrial fibrillation or other anticoagulation indications, prior revascularization, drug interactions, pregnancy potential where relevant, cost, and current guidelines. Do not independently combine or discontinue antithrombotic agents without understanding the indication and coordinating with the relevant clinician.

For chronic symptomatic PAD, supervised exercise therapy or a structured community-based program with behavioral support can improve walking performance, function, and quality of life. The patient needs a practical plan for pain, mobility, transportation, footwear, glucose control, wound care, and safe activity—not only the instruction to “walk more.”

Part 6 — Foot Protection and Team Care

At every relevant visit, inspect the feet or confirm a reliable foot-care plan, especially in diabetes, neuropathy, prior amputation, or known PAD. Teach daily self-inspection when feasible, prompt reporting of wounds/color change/new pain, skin and nail safety, footwear protection, and avoidance of thermal injury. Coordinate vascular specialists, podiatry, wound care, diabetes care, rehabilitation, cardiology, and social services as needed. Foot care is not cosmetic; it is limb-preservation care.

Clinical Case

A 69-year-old with diabetes, CKD, and tobacco exposure has a painful toe ulcer that has not healed for six weeks. The foot is cool, pulses are difficult to detect, and pain worsens at night.

FNP reasoning: this is concerning for CLTI, potentially complicated by infection and neuropathy. Assess systemic and local infection, perfusion, tissue loss, pain, and urgent risk; obtain/coordinate appropriate vascular assessment rather than treating the wound in isolation. Ensure timely multidisciplinary limb-salvage pathway and clear emergency precautions.

FNP PAD Framework

  1. Classify the presentation: asymptomatic, chronic symptomatic, CLTI, or ALI.
  2. Compare trajectory: walking limitation, rest pain, wounds, neurologic change, and abrupt versus chronic onset.
  3. Examine both legs and feet: perfusion, skin/tissue, pulses, sensation, wounds, infection, and footwear.
  4. Confirm and stage appropriately: ABI and further testing/referral guided by the clinical question and urgency.
  5. Protect life and limb: cardiovascular prevention, tobacco treatment, structured exercise, foot care, medication safety, and urgent vascular escalation when indicated.

High-Yield Summary

PAD: increases both limb and cardiovascular risk.
Claudication: is exertional, reproducible, and rest-relieved—but differentials remain broad.
ABI: helps establish PAD when history/exam is suggestive; interpret it in context.
CLTI: rest pain, nonhealing wound, or gangrene requires urgent limb-preservation evaluation.
ALI: sudden pain/coolness/pulse or neurologic change is an emergency.
FNP standard: protect the foot, function, and cardiovascular future while addressing access and social barriers.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. PAD testing, antithrombotic selection, exercise advice, wound care, revascularization referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
